newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ITU chief sees chances low for WTO telecom pact.
newsitem.headline: ITU chief sees chances low for WTO telecom pact.

text.p: The chief of the International Telecommunications Union (ITU) said on Wednesday he was not optimistic a global trade pact in the sector could be wrapped up by the latest deadline of February 15 next year.

Negotiations on opening up lucrative telecom markets in developed and developing countries have been under way in the World Trade Organisation for over two years and officials have recently voiced hopes a deal could be finalised.

"I am still not very optimistic about the February 15 deadline in the WTO negotiations," ITU Secretary-General Pekka Tarjanne told reporters at the end of a conference at the United Nations agency on mobile satellite phone links.
"There appears to be no rush of offers. People are waiting for each other to come forward. It is hard to believe that there would be a major breakthrough by the middle of February."

Although Tarjanne's agency -- which works to improve global cooperation in the use and improvement of telecoms -- is not directly involved in the WTO talks, ITU officials have closely followed progress.
But WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell expressed surprise at the the Finnish ITU chief's comments.

"It is very early to make such a determination, particularly given the improved outlook regarding satellites and the commitments taken by the United States and the European Union in Seattle (in September)," he said.
The two top trade powers agreed at a meeting in the U.S. city also attended by Canada and Japan that they would make a major effort to help shape a pact in the 125-member WTO by the deadline.

Reports over the past few days have suggested that a lowering of one of the major barriers to a deal -- resistance by major U.S. satellite communications companies -- had raised hopes that it could be completed in time.

Trade sources said that at a meeting of the WTO's telecoms working group last Friday, both U.S. and EU negotiators promised they would be coming forward with new offers on market openings in the next few weeks.

The pact, part of unfinished business from the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of global trade negotiations, was originally due to have been finalised by April 30 this year, but the United States pulled out at the last moment.
U.S. negotiators said offers on the table, especially from key emerging economies in Asia and Latin America, were not sufficient for Washington to agree to open up wide the U.S. domestic market.

But all delegations to the talks, in which 48 countries including the 14 EU members have offers on the table, agreed to set their sights on a new deadline -- two months after the WTO's first ministerial conference in Singapore in December.

The EU, whose Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has been one of the chief proponents of an accord, is understood to have told last Friday's WTO meeting that more progress to a deal could be made when the working group next met on November 15.
Trade sources said both U.S. and EU officials clearly felt the Singapore ministerial could give the political impetus needed to complete a pact by mid-February.
